sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Car parks in Düsseldorf were busier in 2024 than at any point since 2020, about 7% above 2023, and have fallen back since: 2025 was level with 2023 and the first nine months of 2026 ran 3% below the same months of 2025, a little weaker than Germany as a whole (−2%).

The city has been tightening on-street parking in small steps rather than closing the centre to cars. In 2019 the administration proposed raising the inner-city street tariff from €2.90 to €4.00 an hour [0], and in 2020 it decided to add 25 resident-parking zones to the existing 31 [1]. Resident permits are the political sticking point: the mayor froze a planned rise in 2022, citing household energy costs [5], and in 2023 the CDU–Green coalition proposed lifting the €25 annual permit to €240–360 [6]. The 2021 settlement of the air-quality lawsuit ruled out driving bans and instead committed to signal control, park-and-ride and a new U81 light-rail line to the fairground and airport [4].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
The garage market has changed hands more than it has grown. APCOA took over the 660-space KII/Schauspielhaus garage in 2020 and fitted plate recognition and occupancy-based pricing [2]; Q-Park took the former Karstadt garage on Liesegangstraße in 2021 and renamed it Stadtmitte [3]; and APCOA added the Medical Center garage in 2024, its tenth site in the city [9]. Both Galeria department stores survived the 2024 insolvency [10]. Shopping-centre garages vary widely in our data: the former Karstadt garage, now Stadtmitte, is 39% occupied on weekdays, the Kö-Galerie garage only 4%.

Charging is being added garage by garage rather than in one programme: Contipark and E.ON plan around 30 points per site [7], IDR opened a charging park of more than 60 points on the Carlsplatz roof [8], and APCOA opened nine in 2025 [11].

sections.title: Operators, location, price and use
sections.text:
Q-Park is the largest operator, with about half of the short-stay spaces the city publishes, followed by Contipark and APCOA; Goldbeck, IDR and a few independents make up the rest. Prices fall with distance from the Königsallee: within 500 m the typical garage charges €3.35 an hour and €30 a day, beyond 2 km €2.00 and €15.

The operators position themselves differently. APCOA is the most central (63% of its spaces within 1 km) and the dearest, about 7% above its immediate neighbours, yet its garages we measure are among the emptiest (20% on weekdays; KII/Schauspielhaus 6%). Q-Park prices in line with its neighbours and sits at 27%. Contipark clusters around the main station, which is the busiest part of town (57%). Goldbeck and IDR undercut their neighbours by 20–25% and are fuller (36–41%), and the busiest garage of all is B+B's Ratinger Tor (63%). Across the city, price and occupancy are unrelated: being dearer does not empty a garage here, and being cheaper does not fill it.
